consensus_summary: Sheol is the OT common realm/abode of the dead (grave or underworld) to which all, righteous and wicked, descend; a shadowy/silent condition or intermediate state corresponding to Hades, distinct from Gehenna/final punishment. Consciousness, compartments, and exact nature remain disputed across traditions.
book_summary: Sheol is the demanding place (etym. sha'al ‘to demand’): mortality’s claim that swallows all flesh alike, personified with mouth/gates/bars. Its dead sleep in silence until released; then Sheol itself is destroyed. Distinct from Gehenna.
consensus_core_identification: common abode/realm of the dead (the grave/underworld) for all people
book_core_identification: mortality’s demanding claim/place that swallows all the dead (who sleep silently) until it is destroyed
boundary_disagreement: Book treats silent sleep of the dead plus Sheol’s own later destruction as definitional; consensus leaves consciousness open (primary often neutral or shadowy, sleep only an alternative) and treats destruction mainly as a later NT note rather than core to the OT term.
rationale: Both identify the same central referent—the shared destination of all the dead, distinct from Gehenna. The book preserves that referent while tightening precision around etymology (‘demand’), universal claim, personification, sleep, and eventual destruction; these are present in consensus notes or alternatives but not required by the primary consensus core. No replacement of the referent occurs, only boundary/precision refinement.
strongest_objection: Standard scholarship regards the etymology of Sheol as uncertain and does not make ‘demand’ or definitional soul-sleep central, so the book’s tighter portrait may over-specify a contested minority reading.
